source_text: ζήσωμεν, ποιήσομεν τοῦτο ἢ ἐκεῖνο, νῦν δὲ καυχᾶσθε ἐν ταῖς ἀλαζονείαις ὑμῶν.» Οὐκοῦν ἰχθύων διανηχόμεθα δίκην τὴν πλατεῖαν ταύτην καὶ εὐρύχωρον θάλασσαν, τοῦτ' ἔστι, τὸν κόσμον· διάφορος γάρ πως ὁ ἑκάστου βίος. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ εἰσάπαν ἀπονενεύκασιν ἐπὶ τὸ χρῆναι πλημμελεῖν, ἀλλ' ἴσασι μὲν, ἀῤῥωστοῦντες ἔσθ' ὅτε, καὶ ταῖς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐνεχόμενοι πλεονεξίαις, καὶ οὐκ ἀφεστάναι τῶν ἄλλων αἰτιαμάτων βούλονται. «Πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες,» κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Ἀποσείονται δ' οὖν ὅμως ὡς ἀκαλλὲς τὸ γυμνῶς ἐθέλειν ἀσχημονεῖν. Ἀναπείσειε δ' ἂν οὐδεὶς ἐμφανῆ τε καὶ ἀκατάσκιον ἐπιτηδεύειν τὴν πλημμέλειαν. Ἐπιμελοῦνται δὲ σφόδρα τοῦ χρῆναι λαθεῖν. «Σοφοὶ γὰρ κρύψουσι τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας,» κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Τοῦτο, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ ὡς ἐν τάξει κατακαλύμματος τὰς λεπίδας ἔχειν. Ἀνανήχονται δὲ πλειστάκις καὶ εἰς τὸ ὑψοῦ, βλέπουσι γὰρ, οὐκ εἰς τὸ κάτω διὰ παντὸς, φρονοῦσι δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄνω, καὶ διαδιδράσκουσιν εὐπετῶς τοὺς οἵπερ ἂν ἕλοιντο σαγηνεύειν εἰς ὄλεθρον· τοῦτό τις ἐρεῖ τὸ οἱονεὶ πτερυγίοις κεχρῆσθαι νοητῶς, καὶ θερμὴν ἄγαν τὴν τῆς διανοίας ποιεῖσθαι κίνησιν. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εἰκότα ἔφης· ἀποφέρει γάρ πως τὸ αἴνιγμα πρὸς τὸ τῇδε ἔχειν οἴεσθαι τὸν λόγον. {ΚΥΡ.} Πλημμελοῦσι δέ τινες, οὐχ ὑπεσταλμένως, γυμνὴν δὲ ὥσπερ καὶ ἀκατακάλυπτον παντελῶς ἐπιτηδεύοντες τὴν φαυλότητα· καὶ περὶ αὐτῶν ἂν λέγοιτο καλῶς· «Ὧν ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ αἰσχύνῃ αὐτῶν.» Νενεύκασι γὰρ ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀκαθαρσίαν, καὶ τοῖς κατωτάτω βορβόροις ἐγκαλινδούμενοι, κνώδαλα κατὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς, ἤγουν, ἕτερόν τι παρὰ τοῦτό εἰσιν. Εἶεν δ' ἂν οἱ τοιοίδε πάντη τε καὶ πάντως ἀδρανεῖς τε καὶ εὐάλωτοι, ταῖς εἰς πᾶν ὁτιοῦν τῶν ἐκτόπων ἡδοναῖς τυραννούμενοι. Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ τοιουτοσί πώς ἐστι τῶν ἀπεγνωσμένων ὁ βίος; Γύναιά τε γὰρ τὰ μαχλῶντα καὶ ἑταιριζόμενα, καὶ τὸ πάναισχρόν τε καὶ κιβδηλότατον τῶν θηλυδρίων γένος, καὶ μὴν καὶ ὅσοι διαπρέπουσιν ἐν σκηναῖς, καὶ οἷς ἀκόρεστος ἡ φιλοσαρκία, καὶ τὸ πλανᾶσθαι φίλον εἰς βέβηλον εἰδωλολατρίαν, ἐπάρατον ἀληθῶς διαζῶσι βίον, καὶ τὸν εἰς αἰσχροτάτους ἥκοντα μολυσμούς. Οὐκοῦν καθαρίζει μὲν ὁ νόμος τοὺς ἠῤῥωστηκότας μὲν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, μὴ μὴν ἔτι καὶ εἰσάπαν ἐκτετραμμένους, ἀνανηχομένους δὲ ὥσπερ εἰς τὸ ὑψοῦ, καὶ οὐχὶ τοῖς ἐπιγείοις ἐνιζήσαντας μόνοις, πεφρονηκότας δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄνω, καὶ μεμερισμένους ὥσπερ Θεῷ τε καὶ κόσμῳ. Καταμιαίνει δὲ αὐτοὺς ὅλῳ χωροῦντας τρόπῳ, πρὸς τὸ ἀκαταλήκτως ἑλέσθαι καὶ δρᾷν καὶ φρονεῖν τὰ σαρκός τε καὶ κόσμου, καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις μὲν ἅπασαν ἀποδυσαμένους αἰδῶ, γυμνῶς δὲ καὶ ἀπημφιεσμένως ἀσχημονεῖν εἰωθότας. Ἐξίστησι δὲ χρησίμως τῆς πρὸς αὐτοὺς κοινωνίας, τὴν πρὸς ἐκείνους οὐκ ἀτιμάζων. Οὐ γάρ τοι τοῖς φαύλοις ἰέναι κατὰ ταυτὸν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς
pass_a_gloss: [continuing the James quotation] ...we shall live, we shall do this or that; but now you boast in your arrogances. Therefore after the manner of fish we swim through this broad and wide sea, that is, the world; for somehow the life of each one is different. For some have not wholly inclined toward the need to sin wrongly, but they know, being weak at times and held fast by the greedinesses of the flesh, and they do not wish to stand apart from the other charges either. 'For we all stumble in many things,' according to what is written. Yet they shake off, as a thing unlovely, the wish to behave shamefully nakedly. And no one would persuade them to practice wrongdoing that is plain and unshaded. They take great care about the need to escape notice. 'For the wise will hide their own shames,' according to what is written. This, I think, is to have the scales as in the rank of a covering. They swim up very often also toward the height; for they look not downward through everything, but they also mind the things above, and they easily run away from those who would choose to catch them in a net for destruction; this one will call to use fins, as it were, in the mind's sense, and to make the movement of the understanding very warm. PALLADIUS: You said fitting things; for the riddle somehow carries one toward thinking that the account holds this way. CYRIL: But some sin, not in a held-back way, practicing their baseness naked as it were and altogether uncovered; and about them it would be said well: 'Whose glory is in their shame.' For they have bent always toward uncleanness, and rolling themselves in the lowest mud, they are wild beasts according to the truth, or something other beside this. Such ones would be in every way and altogether powerless and easily caught, tyrannized by the pleasures toward anything whatever of the outrageous things. Or is not the life of the despaired-of somehow of this kind? For lewd women and women playing the courtesan, and the all-shameful and most counterfeit race of effeminate men, and indeed also as many as are conspicuous on the stages, and those for whom love of flesh is insatiable, and to whom wandering into profane idolatry is dear: they live through a life truly accursed, and the one that has come to most shameful defilements. Therefore the law cleanses those who have been weak in human things, not however also wholly turned aside, but swimming up as it were toward the height, and not having settled on the earthly things alone, but having minded also the things above, and divided as it were between God and world. But it defiles those going over in a whole manner toward choosing unceasingly both to do and to think the things of flesh and of world, and in these having stripped off all shame, and accustomed to behave shamefully nakedly and unclothed. And it usefully removes from the fellowship toward them, not dishonoring the one toward those others. For it is not safe to go the same way with the base, but with the [next section: more decent].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …we will live, and we will do this or that.” But as it is, you boast in your arrogance’ (James 4:15–16). So then, like fish, we swim through this broad and spacious sea, that is, the world (Psalm 104:25); for each person’s life differs in some way. For some have not wholly given themselves over to sin. They know, indeed, that at times they are weak and held by the greedy cravings of the flesh, and they do not claim to be clear of other faults either; for ‘we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2), as it is written. All the same, they shake off as something ugly any wish to behave shamefully with nothing to cover them, and no one could persuade them to practice their wrongdoing openly and without concealment. They take great care to escape notice; for ‘the wise will hide their own shame’ (Proverbs 12:16), as it is written. This, I think, is what it means to have scales as a kind of covering. They also very often swim up toward the heights; for they do not always look downward, but also set their minds on the things above (Colossians 3:2), and they easily slip away from those who would wish to net them for destruction. This, one may say, is to use fins, as it were, in a spiritual sense, and to make the movement of the mind very fervent.
Palladius: What you say is reasonable; for the riddle does in some way lead one to think that the meaning runs this way.

Cyril: But some sin with no restraint, practicing their wickedness naked, as it were, and wholly uncovered; and of them it may well be said, ‘Their glory is in their shame’ (Philippians 3:19). For they are always bent toward uncleanness, and as they wallow in the lowest mire they are in truth brute beasts, or something other than that. Such people would be utterly feeble in every way and easily caught, ruled like slaves of a tyrant by pleasures that lead to every kind of outrage. Or is not the life of those given up as lost something like this? Lewd women and harlots, the utterly shameful and most counterfeit tribe of effeminate men, those who make a name for themselves on the stage, those whose love of the flesh cannot be satisfied, and those who love to wander off into profane idolatry: all these live a truly accursed life, a life that sinks into the most shameful defilements. So the law declares clean those who have been weak in human ways but have not yet turned aside altogether; who swim up, as it were, toward the heights, and have not settled on earthly things alone, but have also set their minds on the things above, and are divided, as it were, between God and the world. But it declares unclean those who give themselves over entirely to choosing, without ceasing, both to do and to think the things of the flesh and of the world; who in these matters have stripped off all shame and are used to behaving shamefully, naked and undisguised. And it usefully removes us from fellowship with these, while not dishonoring fellowship with the former. For to walk the same road as the wicked is not safe; but with those…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Pass A rewritten 2026-10-23 as a plain English sense gloss of the Greek: the reviewed gloss interleaved Greek phrases with English, and once the Greek tags moved into lemmas[] too little English was left. Meaning unchanged; Pass B not touched.

Section opens mid-quotation (James 4:13–16 begins in section 21) and mid-turn of Cyril; it carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label used by the other rows of this book, and the inner and outer quotation marks close those opened in section 21. The sea image echoes Psalm 104:25 (LXX 103:25), quoted in section 21. The old English swapped the two references: ‘we all stumble in many ways’ is James 3:2; ‘the wise will hide their own shame’ is a loose quotation closest in sense to Proverbs 12:16 (LXX: the prudent man hides his own dishonour), though its opening words match LXX Proverbs 10:14 (‘the wise will hide perception’). ‘They do not claim to be clear of other faults’ takes βούλονται + ἀφεστάναι as ‘mean/claim’; a more literal sense is ‘they do not wish to stand apart from the other charges’. ‘Set their minds on the things above’ (τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖν) is cited at its first occurrence (Colossians 3:2); the repeat later in the section is left uncited. ‘The things of the flesh’ (τὰ σαρκός φρονεῖν) may echo Romans 8:5 but is left uncited as doubtful. κνώδαλα is rendered ‘brute beasts’; ‘or something other than that’ renders ἤγουν ἕτερόν τι παρὰ τοῦτο, whose referent is unclear (perhaps ‘other than fish’ in the type). ‘Removes us’: the Greek has no expressed object. καθαρίζει / καταμιαίνει are rendered ‘declares clean / declares unclean’, since the law’s verdict on clean and unclean creatures is meant. The section ends mid-sentence; it completes in section 23.
γυμνὴν … τὴν φαυλότητα: nakedness belongs to the wickedness (‘naked, as it were, and wholly uncovered’)
checked James 4:15–16, Psalm 104:25 (LXX 103:25), James 3:2, Proverbs 12:16 (loose; see note), Colossians 3:2, Philippians 3:19; trailing ‘…’ added for the mid-sentence break
